manuscript_title: Evaluating the Impact of Epidemic Control via

required_revisions.text: Deposit the processed weekly incidence data, the recursion/solver code, and the calibration scripts in a versioned public repository with a DOI (e.g. Zenodo release tied to a tagged GitHub commit), and cite the DOI in a revised Data and Code Availability section. Replace the 'upon reasonable request' wording entirely.

Add a validation subsection (new appendix or Section 3.1 addendum) benchmarking the recursion-derived PMF of C_I, the extinction-time moments, and the inverted density for the fitted N=63, P=3 Luxembourg configuration and for a small synthetic P=2 case against (i) direct sparse solution of the global generator system and (ii) Monte Carlo simulation of the CTMC with reported Monte Carlo error bars. Report maximum absolute/relative discrepancies.

Validate the Abate–Whitt inversion against a case with a known or independently simulated extinction-time density (e.g. the one-phase SIR), report the maximum relative inversion error, and state explicitly in each affected figure caption how many grid points were set to zero because of negative or non-finite inversion output.

In the revised Methods, state the programming language and library versions (e.g. Python/NumPy/SciPy with version numbers), the hardware or runtime environment, the fixed random seed(s) used for the L-BFGS-B multistart, the number of starts, and whether reported estimates come from a single run or are the best over starts. This closes the two HARD methods-completeness gaps.

Add a sensitivity analysis (supplementary table or figure) reporting E[C_I], E[T] and Corr(T,C_I) for γ ∈ {1/4, 1/3, 1/2}, q ∈ {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.35}, ψ ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.10}, and the Eq. 19 coefficients perturbed by ±50%, and state in the text whether the qualitative ranking of scenarios is stable under these perturbations.

Reframe the title and abstract so the conditional scope precedes the effect language: adopt the proposed retitle (or equivalent wording that removes the historical-evaluation reading) and move the sentence stating that switching mechanisms are specified rather than estimated ahead of the sentence describing what the results show.

Verify and update the publication status of Papageorgiou (2025, 2026a, 2026b), supplying DOIs or acceptance details; mark unpublished items as 'manuscript in preparation' and remove any that support load-bearing claims. Also correct or explain the future-dated access dates for Mathieu et al. (2022) and WHO (2024).

Add a paragraph in the related-work discussion comparing Feng & Wang (2023) on switching state-space transmission models to the present finite-population CTMC construction, stating the difference in state representation and in distributional versus point-estimate output.

Add the robustness check re-fitting the one-phase model with the two partial weeks excluded, reporting (b̂, Ŝ(0), Î(0)) alongside the main estimates, and state the exact partial-week aggregation rule used in the Poisson likelihood.

Incorporate into Section 3.6 the argument given in the rebuttal that the near-invariance of Corr(T,C_I) across scenarios is a substantive result — showing that mechanisms which shift E[C_I] without shifting E[T] nonetheless preserve strong positive dependence — so that the value of the joint machinery is stated in the paper rather than left implicit.

minor_suggestions: Surface the O(P^3N^2 + P^2N^3) versus O(|S_T|^3) complexity comparison in the Introduction's contributions paragraph, with a forward pointer to Section 2.4.
Add the one-sentence gloss on the purpose of Φ_{s,i,p}(z,u) immediately after Eq. (4), and define μ^{(k,r)}_{s,i,p} = E[T^k(N_I)^r | (s,i,p)] at first use rather than only before Theorem 4.
Revise the Figure 2 caption to name the observation model and the time unit, as proposed.
Standardise on 'extinction time' throughout, replacing 'epidemic duration' and 'outbreak duration'.
Consider whether the Papageorgiou (2026a) citation on terrorism radicalization is germane in the scope discussion; if retained, make the relevance to the present construction explicit in one clause.
State the exact download date and, if available, the file version or snapshot of the Our World in Data mpox series used, so the input series can be reconstructed independently of upstream revisions.

weaknesses.text: The central methodological claim—that the recursion 'replaces a large global linear system with small phase-level solves'—is stated in the abstract but its practical significance is not quantified until Section 2.4 (page 14), where the computational complexity is given as O(P³N²) for the recursion versus O(|S_T|³) for a dense global solve. A reader cannot judge the contribution's importance until late in the paper. Suggest moving or emphasizing the complexity comparison earlier.

In Section 2.2, the joint transform Φ_{s,i,p}(z,u) is introduced (equation 4) as 'the joint Laplace–Stieltjes transform–probability generating function of (T, N_I)', but the practical meaning—what questions this object answers—is deferred to Section 2.3 (Corollary 3). A sentence like 'From this transform we can extract the marginal distributions of extinction time and infection count, as well as their dependence' would clarify purpose before derivation.

Quantitative comparisons in Section 3 sometimes lack precision. For example, 'earlier intervention shifts the distribution of C_I towards smaller values' (page 20) is directional but the next sentence gives means (33.52 vs 21.82). However, the phrase 'shifts the distribution' without stating the shift magnitude (e.g., 'reduces the mean by 35%') makes the claim less concrete. This is SOFT but repeated across scenarios.

Figure 2 caption states 'Bars represent the observations, and the solid line represents the fitted means' but does not specify the observation model (Poisson) or the time unit (weeks). A reader must cross-reference to Section 3.1 to understand what is plotted. Suggest: 'Observed weekly mpox incidence (bars) and fitted Poisson means (line) under the one-phase baseline SIR model.'

The notation for mixed moments μ^{(k,r)}_{s,i,p} is introduced in Section 2.3 but its interpretation (E[T^k (N_I)^r]) is given only in the text before Theorem 4. The notation itself does not signal that it is a mixed moment; a brief gloss at first use (e.g., 'mixed moments μ^{(k,r)}_{s,i,p} = E[T^k (N_I)^r]') would help.

In Section 3.5, the state-dependent escalation rate λ^{sd}_{1,2}(s,i) = 0.01 + 0.40 i²/(i² + 62) is presented without justification for the functional form or the constants. The caption to Figure 9 states 'Rates are expressed in week⁻¹' but does not explain why this particular sigmoid-like function was chosen or how sensitive results are to the choice. This is not a HARD clarity issue (the formula is stated) but it creates friction for a reader trying to understand the design.

The paper uses 'extinction time' and 'epidemic duration' interchangeably (e.g., page 3: 'the time until extinction are random'; page 26: 'outbreak duration'). While context makes the meaning clear, consistent terminology would reduce friction. Recommend settling on one term throughout.

In Theorem 2, the recursion (equations 6–7) is stated for Φ_{s,i}(z,u) but the boundary condition Φ_{s,0}(z,u) = 1_P is stated only after the theorem statement. A reader must infer that i=0 is a base case. Suggest: 'with boundary condition Φ_{s,0}(z,u) = 1_P for all s.'

questions: In Section 2.1, you state that 'the phase coordinate alone need not be Markovian; the joint process X is Markovian.' Can you clarify with a concrete example whether the state-dependent switching rates λ_{p,p'}(s,i) in your application (Scenario 4, equation 19) are chosen to ensure the joint process remains Markovian, or is this automatic by construction?

Section 3.1 fixes the mean infectious period at γ = 1/3 per week 'consistently with the reported two-to-four-week duration' but then states this is 'a pragmatic calibration assumption rather than as a direct estimate.' How sensitive are the scenario comparisons in Section 3 to this choice? Would γ = 1/4 or γ = 1/2 materially change the conclusions?

In the empirical application, you calibrate only the baseline one-phase model to data and then specify the switching mechanisms exogenously. You acknowledge this ('the switching intensities and intervention effects are specified rather than estimated'). But could you briefly discuss what data or additional information would be needed to estimate the switching rates λ_{p,p'}(s,i) from observed intervention histories?

Figure 5 and Figure 10 show PMFs of C_I under different scenarios. The x-axis ranges differ between figures (e.g., Figure 5 goes to ~80, Figure 10 to ~60). Was this intentional to show the full support, or would a consistent x-axis range across all infection-count figures aid comparison?

In Section 2.4, you state the cost is 'O(P³N² + P²N³) for fixed i_0.' Can you clarify whether this is the cost to compute all moments up to a fixed order (k,r), or the cost per (z,u) evaluation? This affects the practical utility claim.

weaknesses.text: The empirical application does not fit the regime-switching model to data; instead, a one-phase baseline is calibrated and then alternative mechanisms are evaluated conditionally on fitted parameters. This design choice is disclosed but limits the inferential scope: competing intervention scenarios cannot be empirically ranked, and the practical utility of the framework for real policy evaluation remains undemonstrated (Section 3 and Discussion).

The fixed infectious period (γ=1/3 per week, corresponding to 3 weeks) is stated as 'a pragmatic calibration assumption rather than as a direct estimate' (Section 3.1), but no sensitivity analysis is provided to show how results change if this assumption is relaxed. Given that the reported confidence interval for bI(0) is wide [0.06,1.12], sensitivity to the recovery rate would be informative.

The numerical inversion of the Laplace–Stieltjes transform for extinction-time densities uses the Abate–Whitt method with standard parameters (A≈18.4, 15 initial terms, 11 Euler averaging terms). No validation of inversion accuracy is provided (e.g., comparison to analytical results for simple cases, or sensitivity to the number of terms). The statement that 'numerical values that were non-finite or negative only because of inversion error were set to zero before plotting' (Section 3) indicates post-hoc correction of numerical artifacts, which could mask convergence issues.

The mpox data consist of only K=14 weekly observations (16 June to 13 September 2022), which is a small sample for calibration. The fitted model 'provides a reasonable parsimonious representation of the overall epidemic curve' but 'main discrepancies concern local week-to-week fluctuations' (Section 3.1 and Figure 2). No formal goodness-of-fit test (e.g., likelihood-ratio test against a saturated model, or simulation-based posterior predictive check) is reported; the assessment is visual only.

The paper acknowledges that 'the first and last aggregated weeks in the mpox incidence series are partial weeks' and that they 'were retained to preserve the complete observation window' but notes this 'may introduce a small edge effect in the baseline calibration' (Discussion). No analysis of this edge effect is provided; it is unclear whether excluding these weeks would materially change the fitted parameters or subsequent scenario results.

The integer rounding of continuous MLEs (S(0)=62 from 61.88, I(0)=1 from 0.28) is necessary for the finite-state model but introduces a small discontinuity. The impact of this rounding on the reported distributional quantities is not quantified; it is unclear whether results are robust to alternative rounding rules (e.g., rounding I(0) to 0 and checking if the absorbing state is reached immediately).

The scenario parameters (transmission reductions of 25% and 50%, switching rates q=0.35 and q=0.05, vaccination rate ψ=0.05, state-dependent escalation coefficients in Eq. 19) are described as 'illustrative' and 'chosen to separate effects' (Section 3.1). No justification is provided for these specific values, and no sensitivity analysis explores how results change across a range of plausible intervention intensities. The practical relevance of the scenarios to real policy decisions is therefore unclear.

questions: How sensitive are the reported distributional quantities (means, standard deviations, correlations of T and CI) to the fixed infectious period γ=1/3? A one-way sensitivity analysis varying γ over a plausible range (e.g., 1/4 to 1/2 per week) would strengthen confidence in the baseline calibration.

The Abate–Whitt inversion of the Laplace–Stieltjes transform is applied to compute extinction-time densities (Figures 4, 6, 8, 11). Can the authors provide validation of this inversion for a simple case (e.g., a one-phase SIR model with known analytical solution) to demonstrate accuracy? Alternatively, how sensitive are the reported density shapes to the number of inversion terms?

The mpox data consist of only 14 weekly observations. Did the authors consider fitting a richer model (e.g., SEIR with latency, or a two-phase model with an early intervention phase) to the same data to assess whether the one-phase baseline is adequate? A likelihood-ratio test or information criterion comparison would be informative.

For the integer rounding of initial conditions (S(0)=62 from 61.88, I(0)=1 from 0.28), how do results change if I(0) is rounded to 0 and the process is initialized in the absorbing state? This would clarify whether the lower bound of one infectious individual materially affects the scenario comparisons.

The state-dependent escalation function (Eq. 19) is λsd₁,₂(s,i)=0.01+0.40i²/(i²+62). How were the coefficients 0.01, 0.40, and 62 chosen? A sensitivity analysis varying these parameters would show whether the qualitative findings (e.g., state-dependent escalation reduces CI while leaving mean T nearly unchanged) are robust.

In Scenario 4, the state-dependent escalation rate produces a mean CI of 28.50 (vs. 33.52 for constant delayed rate) and a mean T of 14.44 weeks (vs. 14.39 weeks). Given the small sample size and the width of the confidence intervals, is this difference in CI practically meaningful? A formal hypothesis test or equivalence test would clarify.

The paper states that 'the switching intensities and intervention effects are specified rather than estimated from the intervention history' (Abstract). Could the authors outline a path forward for fitting the full regime-switching model to richer data (e.g., daily case counts, hospitalization data, documented intervention dates)? This would help readers understand the practical applicability of the framework.

weaknesses.text: The manuscript does not explicitly state that the work is exempt from IRB/ethics-committee review because it uses only aggregate public data with no human subjects, identifiable information, or interventional components. While this exemption is reasonable and the work appears compliant, an explicit statement of exemption would strengthen transparency (SOFT).

Code availability is stated as 'available from the authors upon reasonable request' rather than deposited in a public repository with a persistent identifier (e.g., GitHub with DOI, Zenodo). For a computational methods paper, immediate public access to code would better support reproducibility (SOFT).

The manuscript does not acknowledge any use of artificial intelligence, machine learning, or large language models in the writing, analysis, or code generation. If none were used, an explicit statement would be appropriate for current standards (SOFT).

questions: Would the authors be willing to deposit the processed data and code in a public repository (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo, or a discipline-specific archive) with a persistent identifier, to facilitate immediate reproducibility and long-term archival?

Can the authors confirm that no IRB or ethics-committee review was sought or required because the work uses only publicly available, non-identifiable aggregate data and involves no human subjects, clinical interventions, or identifiable information?

Were any AI tools, large language models, or automated code-generation systems used in the preparation of this manuscript or its computational implementation? If so, please disclose their role and any limitations they may introduce.

weaknesses.text: Self-citation is moderately high (~8 self-citations, ~16% of the reference list), including several future-dated works (Papageorgiou 2025, 2026a, 2026b, 2026). The publication status of these should be verified; if they are preprints or in preparation, this violates the guideline against using unpublished work to support load-bearing claims.

The applied epidemiological context is thin: very few citations to epidemiological studies of the 2022–2023 mpox outbreak or to vaccination/immunity literature. However, the authors explicitly frame the application as 'conditional comparisons' rather than causal inference, which limits the scope of what must be cited.

The state-dependent regime-switching literature is not comprehensively surveyed. Beyond Artalejo & Gómez-Corral (2010), the manuscript does not cite other work on state-dependent switching in control theory, queueing, or other fields that might provide relevant methodological context.

The characterization of Almaraz and Gómez-Corral (2018) as using 'Markov-modulated infection and removal processes to accommodate non-exponential waiting-time distributions' (p. 3) cannot be verified from the title alone and should be confirmed.

questions: Can you confirm the publication status of Papageorgiou (2025, 2026a, 2026b, 2026)? Are these accepted/in-press papers, or preprints? If preprints, how do they support the claims in the introduction?

In your characterization of Almaraz and Gómez-Corral (2018) on page 3, you state they use 'Markov-modulated infection and removal processes to accommodate non-exponential waiting-time distributions.' Can you confirm this is an accurate summary of their work?

Have you surveyed the broader literature on state-dependent regime switching in control theory, queueing, or other fields? Are there other relevant references beyond Artalejo & Gómez-Corral (2010) that should be cited to contextualize your state-dependent switching mechanism?

weaknesses.text: HARD: The empirical validation does not test the framework's ability to support causal or comparative claims about interventions. All four scenarios (Scenarios 1–4) specify switching intensities and intervention effects rather than estimating them from the historical intervention record. The design therefore cannot distinguish whether observed differences in outcome distributions arise from the intervention mechanisms specified or from unexamined parameter choices. Specifically, the authors state (Section 3, p. 13): 'the switching intensities and intervention-specific effects are specified rather than estimated from the historical policy process.' This means no comparator intervention scenario is fitted to data; all are hypothetical. The claim that 'state-dependent escalation reduces the infection count by increasing the probability of strict control when the infectious population becomes large' (Section 3.5, p. 24) rests entirely on the specified functional form λ^sd_{1,2}(s,i) = 0.01 + 0.40 i²/(i² + 62), not on evidence that this form is optimal or even plausible given Luxembourg's actual policy.

HARD: No sensitivity analysis on switching parameters. The scenarios use fixed switching rates (q = 0.35 for early, q = 0.05 for delayed escalation; ψ = 0.05 for vaccination) without exploring how results change under reasonable perturbations. For instance, if q = 0.35 were instead 0.25 or 0.50, would the ranking of scenarios or the magnitude of differences in mean C_I and T remain stable? The design does not rule out the possibility that conclusions are artifacts of the particular parameter choices made.

HARD: Single baseline calibration. The one-phase SIR model is fitted once to the Luxembourg data (Section 3.1) with fixed γ = 1/3 per week (a pragmatic assumption, not estimated). All subsequent scenarios condition on this single calibration. The design does not test robustness to alternative baseline fits (e.g., γ estimated from data, or γ ∈ [0.2, 0.5]) or to different observation models. The authors note (p. 15) that the negative-binomial fit reached its upper bound κ_max = 20000, suggesting negligible overdispersion, but this does not rule out model misspecification or sensitivity to the fixed γ assumption.

HARD: No positive control or validation of the recursive method against independent benchmarks. The recursive formulas (Theorems 2–4) are mathematically proven, but the numerical implementation is not validated against an alternative method (e.g., Monte Carlo simulation, matrix exponentiation, or a published benchmark case). The authors provide basic consistency checks (Φ_{s,i,p}(0,1) = 1, Σ_n h^{(n)}_{s,i,p}(0) = 1) but these are necessary conditions, not sufficient validation of correctness. For a finite-population Markov chain with N = 63 and P = 3, a stochastic simulation or alternative solver could serve as a positive control.

SOFT: Limited scope of empirical illustration. The mpox outbreak in Luxembourg is small (N = 63, i_0 = 1, 14 weeks, 55 total cases) and represents a single, recent, well-controlled outbreak. The design does not test whether the framework's insights (e.g., strong positive correlation between T and C_I, or the differential effects of timing vs. intensity) generalize to larger, longer, or more severe outbreaks. The authors acknowledge this (Section 4, p. 27) but do not provide even a second illustrative case or synthetic scenario to probe robustness.

SOFT: No comparison to deterministic or simpler stochastic baselines. The paper does not show whether the distributional insights from the regime-switching framework differ meaningfully from those of a simpler model (e.g., a one-phase stochastic SIR, or a deterministic SIR with uncertainty propagated via perturbation). For instance, would a standard SIR with parameter uncertainty yield similar correlations Corr(T, C_I) ≈ 0.85–0.93 (Section 3.6)? The design does not isolate the added value of the regime-switching structure.

SOFT: Partial weeks in data. The authors note (Section 3.1, p. 15) that the first and last aggregated weeks are partial, retained to preserve the observation window. This may introduce edge effects in the baseline calibration, though the authors acknowledge it as 'a minor limitation.' No robustness check (e.g., excluding partial weeks, or re-fitting with full weeks only) is provided.

SOFT: Numerical inversion of Laplace–Stieltjes transforms. The extinction-time densities (Figures 4, 6, 8, 11) are obtained via the Abate–Whitt method (Section 3, p. 13). The authors set negative or non-finite values to zero 'before plotting' due to inversion error. No error bounds or convergence diagnostics are reported. For a public review, transparency about numerical accuracy would strengthen confidence in the displayed densities.

questions: Can the authors provide a Monte Carlo simulation or alternative numerical solver (e.g., matrix exponentiation) as a positive control to validate the recursive implementation for a representative case (e.g., N = 63, P = 3, one scenario)?

How sensitive are the scenario comparisons (Scenarios 1–4) to the specified switching rates and intervention effects? For instance, if q ∈ {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.35} or ψ ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.10}, how do the rankings and magnitudes of differences in E[C_I] and E[T] change?

How robust are the baseline calibration and subsequent scenario results to the fixed assumption γ = 1/3 per week? What if γ were estimated from the data or allowed to vary in a plausible range [0.2, 0.5]?

Can the authors provide a second empirical illustration (e.g., a different outbreak, a larger population, or a synthetic scenario) to test whether the key findings (e.g., strong T–C_I correlation, differential effects of timing vs. intensity) generalize beyond the Luxembourg mpox case?

Do the extinction-time densities (Figures 4, 6, 8, 11) obtained via Abate–Whitt inversion have quantified error bounds or convergence diagnostics? How many grid points and Euler terms were used, and how sensitive are the displayed curves to these choices?

How would the scenario comparisons change if a simpler stochastic baseline (e.g., one-phase SIR without regime switching, or deterministic SIR with parameter uncertainty) were used as a comparator? Does the regime-switching structure materially alter the distributional insights?

The state-dependent escalation function (Eq. 19, Section 3.5) is chosen to be 'low when the number of infectious individuals is small and increases smoothly as i increases.' What is the justification for this particular functional form, and how sensitive are the results to alternative forms (e.g., linear, exponential, threshold-based)?

weaknesses.text: Insufficient differentiation from Almaraz & Gómez-Corral (2018): The manuscript cites Almaraz & Gómez-Corral (2018) as introducing Markov-modulated infection and removal processes in finite-population SIR, and states their framework uses modulation mainly to generate correlated event times while the present work uses it to represent random or epidemic-responsive intervention changes. However, the mathematical structure is nearly identical: both use a finite-state phase process J(t) that modulates transition intensities, both derive recursive formulas for joint transforms, and both analyze extinction time and final size. The claimed distinction (phases as intervention regimes vs. temporal structure enrichment) is interpretive rather than structural. The manuscript does not provide a head-to-head comparison showing what mathematical or computational capability is new beyond Almaraz & Gómez-Corral (2018).

State-dependent transitions not clearly novel: While state-dependent λ_{p,p'}(s,i) is presented as a contribution, the manuscript cites Artalejo & Gómez-Corral (2010) as introducing state-dependent Markov-modulated mechanisms. The present work applies this existing concept to intervention phases. The novelty appears to be the application and interpretation, not the mathematical mechanism itself.

Limited empirical validation of claimed advantages: The Luxembourg mpox case study does not demonstrate that the framework provides insights unavailable from simpler approaches. The baseline one-phase SIR is fitted deterministically; the switching scenarios are then evaluated conditionally on fitted parameters. No comparison is provided showing that (a) the recursive method is faster/more accurate than direct simulation or (b) the joint distributional analysis reveals intervention differences that marginal analyses would miss. The correlations Corr(T, C_I) reported in Section 3.6 (0.85–0.93) are high across all scenarios, suggesting limited practical differentiation in dependence structure.

Vague claim about level-wise recursion novelty: The manuscript states the recursion replaces a large global linear system with small phase-level solves. However, this is a standard consequence of exploiting block structure in Markov chains; the block-bidiagonal form of Q_T,T follows directly from the monotonicity of S(t), which is not new. The computational advantage is real but not a novel insight.

Preprint search found concurrent work on regime-switching epidemics: The search returned A Switching State-Space Transmission Model for Tracking Epidemics and Assessing Interventions (Feng & Wang, 2023, PPR), which addresses regime switching and intervention assessment. While that work appears to use a different state-space framework, the manuscript does not cite or compare against it, raising questions about awareness of concurrent work in this space.

Empirical application does not test the framework's core claims: The mpox analysis uses only 14 weekly observations and fits a one-phase deterministic SIR. The switching scenarios are then specified (not estimated) and evaluated conditionally. This does not demonstrate that the framework can identify or estimate regime-switching parameters from real data, nor does it show that the joint distributional analysis provides actionable insights beyond what deterministic models or simulation would yield.

questions: Specific mathematical novelty over Almaraz & Gómez-Corral (2018): Can the authors provide a detailed comparison showing which equations, theorems, or computational steps in the present work are genuinely new versus direct applications of Almaraz & Gómez-Corral (2018)? For instance, is Theorem 2 (the recursion for Φ_{s,i,p}) a new derivation or a restatement of their result with state-dependent λ_{p,p'} substituted?

Computational efficiency claim: The manuscript claims O(P³N²) cost vs. O(|S_T|³) for dense solution of the full system. However, sparse solvers can reduce the latter. What is the actual wall-clock speedup of the level-wise recursion vs. a sparse direct solver on realistic problem sizes (e.g., N=100–1000, P=2–5)? Is this speedup demonstrated empirically?

Practical utility of joint distribution: In the mpox scenarios (Section 3), the high correlations Corr(T, C_I) ≈ 0.85–0.93 suggest that T and C_I move together. Does the joint analysis reveal intervention trade-offs (e.g., one regime reduces C_I but increases Var(T)) that would not be apparent from marginal comparisons? If not, what is the practical value of computing the joint distribution?

Why not estimate switching parameters from data?: The authors specify λ_{p,p'} rather than estimate them from the Luxembourg intervention history. Given that the framework is designed to handle state-dependent switching, why not use the mpox data to calibrate a two-phase model (no measures → strict control) and compare its fit to the one-phase baseline? This would test whether the added complexity is justified.

Relationship to Artalejo & Gómez-Corral (2010): The manuscript cites Artalejo & Gómez-Corral (2010) as introducing state-dependent Markov-modulated mechanisms. How does the present state-dependent λ_{p,p'}(s,i) differ from their framework? Is the novelty only in the application to intervention phases?

Concurrent work awareness: The preprint search identified A Switching State-Space Transmission Model for Tracking Epidemics and Assessing Interventions (Feng & Wang, 2023). Is the authors' framework aware of and differentiated from this work? If not, a comparison would strengthen the novelty positioning.

weaknesses.text: Code and processed data are gated behind 'reasonable request': The manuscript states 'The processed data and computer code used to reproduce the numerical results are available from the authors upon reasonable request.' This is a HARD flag for load-bearing artifacts. No repository link, DOI, or accession number is provided. An independent group cannot obtain these without author discretion, violating current reproducibility standards for computational work.

No version control or commit hash: Even if code were deposited, no repository URL, commit hash, or version tag is given. The statement 'available from the authors upon reasonable request' provides no permanent, citable reference.

No computational environment specification: Software versions (Python/R version, NumPy/SciPy versions, optimization library versions) are not stated. The Abate–Whitt inversion is described procedurally but no library or implementation reference is given (e.g., is this a custom implementation or a standard package?).

Raw data processing steps not fully documented: The manuscript states weekly aggregation was performed ('aggregated into calendar weeks using Monday as the week start') but does not specify the exact code or intermediate outputs. The handling of partial weeks is mentioned but the precise aggregation rule is not given (e.g., how are partial-week counts handled in the Poisson likelihood?).

No intermediate outputs or checksums: While three basic sanity checks are mentioned (Φ_{s,i,p}(0,1) = 1, sum of h^(n) = 1, sum of probabilities = 1), no intermediate numerical outputs, checksums, or example computations are provided to verify that an independent implementation produces the same values.

Figures lack explicit traceability to code/data: It is not stated which script or function produces each figure (Figures 2–11). For example, is Figure 2 produced by a deterministic ODE solver, and which code block? Are Figures 3–11 produced by the recursive solver, and in what order?

Numerical inversion grid and tolerance not fully specified: The Abate–Whitt inversion uses a finite grid with 120 points and upper endpoint set to max_j{E_j[T] + 4 SD_j(T)}, but the lower endpoint and spacing rule are not stated. Tolerance for 'non-finite or negative' values is described as 'set to zero before plotting', but no threshold is given.

Rounding and integer conversion rule for initial conditions: The manuscript states 'Ŝ(0) was rounded to the nearest integer, while Î(0) was rounded subject to a lower bound of one infectious individual', but does not specify the exact rounding function (e.g., round-half-up, round-half-to-even). This affects reproducibility of the integer initial state (S(0) = 62, I(0) = 1).

No seed or random-number handling: The optimization uses multiple random starting values ('Additional starting values were generated randomly within the admissible parameter bounds'), but no random seed is stated. This affects reproducibility of the calibration step.

questions: Will the authors deposit code and processed data to a permanent, versioned repository (GitHub with a release tag, Zenodo, or similar) with a DOI before or at publication, rather than gating them behind 'reasonable request'?
What software versions (Python/R, NumPy/SciPy, optimization library, Laplace-inversion library) were used? Was the Abate–Whitt inversion implemented custom or via a published package?

Can the authors provide the exact aggregation rule for partial weeks in the Luxembourg data? Specifically, how are the first (16/06–22/06) and last (07/09–13/09) partial weeks counted in the Poisson likelihood?
What is the random seed (or seed-averaging procedure) used for the random starting values in the L-BFGS-B optimization? This affects reproducibility of the baseline calibration.

Can the authors provide intermediate numerical outputs (e.g., the computed values of Φ_{s,i,p}(z, u) for a small example state, or the extinction-time moments for Scenario 1) so that an independent implementation can be validated?
For the Abate–Whitt inversion, what is the lower endpoint of the time grid, and what tolerance threshold is used to decide whether a value is 'non-finite or negative'?
Which specific script or function produces each of Figures 2–11? Are there intermediate outputs (e.g., the PMF vectors or density arrays) that could be inspected?

The manuscript states the fitted model 'should be interpreted as an effective baseline calibration' rather than a detailed reconstruction. Does this mean the one-phase model is intentionally misspecified to represent the observed data? If so, how does this affect the validity of using the fitted parameters (b̂ = 0.99) as the baseline for the switching scenarios?

weaknesses.text: **HARD: Abstract overclaims causal evaluation.** The abstract states 'The results show how switching mechanisms affect both the total number of infected individuals and the extinction time' (line 11–12 of abstract). This language ('show how…affect') implies causal or empirical evaluation of intervention effects. However, the authors immediately qualify this in the next sentence: 'Since the switching mechanisms are specified rather than estimated from the intervention history, the results are conditional model-based comparisons rather than estimates of the historical effects of interventions in Luxembourg.' This qualification contradicts the headline claim. The abstract should lead with the conditional nature, not bury it. As written, a reader skimming the abstract will infer causal findings about mpox control in Luxembourg, which is false.

**HARD: Introduction misrepresents the empirical scope.** The introduction (Section 1, final paragraph) states: 'To illustrate the method, we use weekly mpox incidence data from Luxembourg to calibrate a baseline one-phase SIR model and then evaluate alternative intervention mechanisms conditionally on the fitted parameters.' This is accurate. However, the preceding sentence claims the framework 'permits full distributional comparisons of intervention mechanisms, including cases in which marginal means are similar but uncertainty or dependence differs.' While true in principle, the empirical section does not compare mechanisms estimated from data; it compares hypothetical scenarios with specified switching rates. The framing suggests the method can empirically evaluate competing interventions, but the case study only demonstrates conditional scenario comparison. This is a genuine limitation that should be foregrounded, not implied to be overcome.

**SOFT: Specification of scenario parameters lacks justification.** Section 3.5 states: 'The intervention-specific values used in Scenarios 1–4 are illustrative and are chosen to separate the effects of intervention intensity, intervention timing, direct immunity acquisition, and state-dependent escalation.' The choices are reasonable for pedagogical separation, but the paper does not justify why these particular parameter values (e.g., ψ = 0.05 for vaccination, λ_sd coefficients in Eq. 19) are plausible for Luxembourg or mpox. The authors acknowledge this ('should therefore be interpreted as conditional model comparisons, not as estimates of the historical effects'), but the lack of sensitivity analysis or range exploration weakens the illustrative power. A brief sensitivity check (e.g., varying ψ or the state-dependent threshold) would strengthen the case study.

**SOFT: Partial weeks in data not fully addressed.** Section 3.1 notes: 'Since the observation window starts on 16/06/2022 and ends on 13/09/2022, the first and last aggregated weeks are partial. These weeks were retained in the calibration.' The authors mention this as a 'minor limitation' in Section 4 but do not quantify its impact. Dropping or downweighting partial weeks, or re-running the baseline fit without them, would clarify whether this edge effect materially affects the fitted parameters (b̂, Ŝ(0), Î(0)) used in all downstream scenarios.

**SOFT: Numerical inversion method not validated.** The Abate–Whitt Euler inversion (Section 3) is applied with standard parameters (A ≈ 18.4, 15 initial terms, 11 Euler averaging terms) but no validation is provided. The authors note 'Numerical values that were non-finite or negative only because of inversion error were set to zero before plotting,' which is a post-hoc correction. A brief check (e.g., comparing inversion results to known closed-form densities for a simple scenario, or reporting relative error bounds) would increase confidence in the plotted densities.

**SOFT: Claim of 'exact' results requires qualification.** The paper repeatedly states results are 'exact up to numerical linear-system solution' (e.g., Section 2, final paragraph; Section 3). This is technically correct but may mislead readers unfamiliar with numerical linear algebra. Condition numbers of the matrices A_{s,i}(z) are not reported, and no error analysis is provided. For large N or P, ill-conditioning could accumulate. A brief note on numerical stability or a condition-number check for the Luxembourg case (N=63, P≤3) would be helpful.

**SOFT: State-dependent escalation function (Eq. 19) appears ad hoc.** The function λ^sd_{1,2}(s,i) = 0.01 + 0.40 i²/(i² + 6²) is presented as illustrative but its form is not motivated. Why a quadratic numerator and denominator? Why the constant 0.01 and coefficient 0.40? The authors state 'The coefficients and threshold in the state-dependent escalation function (19) are chosen so that the transition rate is low when the number of infectious individuals is small and increases smoothly as i increases,' but this describes the qualitative behavior, not the specific parameterization. Sensitivity to these choices is not explored.

questions: In the abstract, can the authors reorder the sentences so that the conditional nature of the comparisons ('specified rather than estimated') appears in the first sentence, not as a qualifier after the headline claim?

Section 3.1 fixes γ = 1/3 per week based on a 'pragmatic calibration assumption' rather than estimation from data. How sensitive are the scenario results (Figures 3–11) to this choice? A brief one-way sensitivity analysis (e.g., γ ∈ [1/4, 1/2]) would clarify robustness.

For the state-dependent escalation function (Eq. 19), can the authors justify the specific form (quadratic numerator/denominator, constants 0.01 and 0.40) or provide a sensitivity analysis showing how the results in Scenario 4 change if the function is replaced by, e.g., a linear or logistic form?

Can the authors quantify the impact of retaining partial weeks in the baseline calibration? Re-fitting the one-phase model excluding the first and last weeks would show whether edge effects materially change b̂, Ŝ(0), Î(0).

The Abate–Whitt inversion is applied with fixed parameters (A ≈ 18.4, 15 terms, 11 Euler weights). For the Luxembourg case, can the authors report the relative error or validate the inversion against a simple closed-form benchmark (e.g., exponential or gamma density)?

In Section 2.4, the authors note that computing the full set of coefficient transforms h^(n)_{s,i,p}(z) has cost O(P³N² + P²N³). For the Luxembourg case (N=63, P=3), can they report actual wall-clock times for computing all scenarios, to help readers assess computational feasibility for larger populations?

The paper claims the framework allows 'policy escalation to react to the number of infectious individuals' (Introduction). However, the state-dependent mechanism in Scenario 4 is the only empirical example. Can the authors discuss or illustrate how the framework would handle other reactive policies, e.g., escalation triggered by cumulative infections or time-since-peak?
